title: What changed when returns, payments and orders were matched
question: Did filed corrections, administrative orders and agency ledgers establish the same amount and outcome?
finding: 14 follow-ups distinguish confirmed transfers, payments, accounting adjustments and unresolved receipts.
how: Check named parties, effective dates and directed payments against the order, reporting form or agency ledger. Compare earlier and amended records separately.
limits: A statutory penalty, a private contribution and a taxpayer loss measure different things. Each row identifies what is still open.

rows.topic: Public Works attributed $123,358 in hospital changes to design errors
rows.record: Public Works identified design errors in the change orders for a rehabilitation project at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital. The Controller’s vouchers trace total payments to the builder.
rows.outstanding: The public tables do not identify a responsible designer, establish negligence, show a recovery, or isolate a payment for each design change.

source.t: Public Works staff report, contract 1000024456, pp. 2–4

rows.topic: Tony Hall’s campaign paid for gifts to his daughters
rows.record: San Francisco’s Ethics Commission found that Tony Hall used $320.36 in campaign funds for gifts and failed to document gasoline expenses. His committee received reimbursement for the gifts almost three years later.
rows.outstanding: The order identifies the time of repayment to the campaign. It supplies no receipt showing when the City collected its $6,000 fine.

source.t: Findings of fact, conclusions of law and order in complaint 24-050928, pages 2–7 and 12–14

rows.topic: Green For All returned its SFPUC payments after a contract conflict
rows.record: Juliet Ellis helped advance a $200,000 SFPUC agreement with a nonprofit that paid her. The joint enforcement record traces two repayments and says SFPUC kept the work.
rows.outstanding: The signed agreement gives the contract value. The reviewed records leave the amount disbursed to the nonprofit and refunded to the City unresolved.

source.t: City stipulation and order, Ellis complaint 11-130606

rows.topic: Two permit consultants disclosed a year of contacts after an investigation
rows.record: The Ethics Commission counted 80 late-reported contacts and $50,675 in consulting fees. The eight corrected reports identify permits with markedly different review times.
rows.outstanding: The record does not establish that the consultants accelerated any permit, that a City official received any consulting fee or that the reported fee was a public loss.

source.t: Amy Lee and Mark Luellen — stipulated decision and order, 20-21-000305

rows.topic: Two union PAC payments missed the pre-election disclosure deadline
rows.record: An audit found that UNITE HERE Local 2 PAC filed rapid disclosures for 20 payments but missed two totaling $9,100. The payments appeared later on its regular campaign statements.
rows.outstanding: The order does not establish that either payment purchased a vote, changed a law, restricted competition or cost the City money.

source.t: Unite Here Local 2 PAC — stipulated decision and order, 16-17-000127

rows.topic: An appeals commissioner reported brokerage income but omitted its sources
rows.record: Darryl Honda disclosed more than $100,000 in annual commission income from his brokerage. A signed Ethics order found that he omitted 37 reportable income sources. Investigators checked those sources against Board of Appeals business.
rows.outstanding: The order identifies no appeals decision involving those income sources and no payment from the City to Honda for the brokerage transactions.

source.t: Darryl Honda — stipulated decision and order, 20-21-000345

rows.topic: A supervisor’s public newsletter list served her reelection campaign
rows.record: District 6 staff helped build a subscriber list for official updates. Campaign newsletters went to that list. The Ethics Commission established a City-resource violation and expressly recorded what staff did at City expense.
rows.outstanding: The record does not establish the value of staff time or that taxpayers paid for the email platform.

source.t: Jane Kim and Jane Kim for Supervisor 2014 — stipulated decision and order, 28-151015

rows.topic: A lobbyist omitted 39 contacts and 35 client payments over seven years
rows.record: A signed order identifies contacts on behalf of Waymo, Apothecarium and the Alameda County Water District. It separates contacts investigators substantiated from $21,050 in payments the lobbyist later disclosed.
rows.outstanding: The order does not show that a City official received the private client payments or changed a decision in return for a contact.

source.t: Michael Colbruno — stipulated decision and order, 19-20-000217

rows.topic: What City College withdrew from its $21 million retiree health authorization
rows.record: The retiree health trust recorded $20,603,414 in two payments to City College. Its financial statements reconcile the second payment to the college’s prior-year accounts.
rows.outstanding: The published figures establish no unauthorized use, theft or loss. The $396,586 is the difference between the ceiling and the disbursements. They do not settle the separate question of long-term funding adequacy.

source.t: Trust board minutes, November 16, 2020, action item 06, PDF p. 5

rows.topic: City College budgeted $32.6 million above its own reserve limit
rows.record: The State Auditor compared the college’s fiscal 2025–26 budget with its board’s 9% maximum. The college later reported an unrestricted balance $12,655,684 above its original projection.
rows.outstanding: A budget-policy difference does not establish missing cash or the denial of a particular student service.

source.t: Board Policy 8.01, budget preparation and fiscal accountability, p. 1

rows.topic: Progress San Francisco reported $1.16 million in contributions to the wrong office
rows.record: Progress San Francisco sent 24 late-contribution disclosures to the state. San Francisco voters were entitled to find them at the city filing office. The Ethics Commission imposed $29,300.
rows.outstanding: The filings do not trace a particular donor’s dollars to a particular expenditure. The settlement concerns disclosure and supplies no evidence of candidate coordination or payment of the penalty.

rows.topic: A joint campaign event turned part of a slate flyer into a $2,613 contribution
rows.record: The Labor & Working Families Slate reported a flyer opposing Bilal Mahmood. The Ethics Commission assigned part of its cost to Dean Preston’s campaign and assessed $2,513.
rows.outstanding: No personal violation was adjudicated against Preston or Jolley. The March amendment preceded the settlement. A later corrective filing or payment receipt requires separate evidence.

rows.topic: Neighbors Advocacy left $100,833 in recall campaign media services off its reports
rows.record: Neighbors for a Better San Francisco Advocacy paid Riff City Strategies to handle media for the Chesa Boudin recall. The Ethics Commission assessed $53,916 for the missing disclosures.
rows.outstanding: The signed order did not establish a violation involving the separate nonprofit’s compensation of Brooke Jenkins. The date the penalty cleared is unresolved.

rows.record: The final audit records $27,894.30 in unexpended public funding returned to the City, $120,043 in public financing and no material audit findings.
rows.outstanding: A separate $2,500 disclosure settlement does not identify the clearing date of its penalty.

source.t: Final campaign audit, Norman Yee for 2012 Supervisor District 7, committee 1342055, section V
